catalogue_metadata.scope_notes: Extraction from the ideas-to-life-cas repository, a Continuous Architecture System (CAS) that uses agentic AI assistants (Claude, Gemini, HuggingFace agents) to govern architecture through a structured knowledge base. Analysis covers source in src/cas_runner, skills/subagents in .agents and .claude, knowledge base layout in cas-knowledge, and CI/CD workflows that drive agentic execution.
analysis_limits: Could not inspect full file contents for all skill markdown files; directory listing and symbol metadata were the primary evidence.
llm/litellm_client.py and runner.py were not read beyond symbol names, so internal flow details are inferred.
The cas-brain/ directory contents were not enumerated; its role as 'brain' is inferred from name and workflow references.
No runtime/execution-profile.yaml contents were available; treated as configuration rather than executable evidence.

system_map.overview: The system is a Continuous Architecture System (CAS) that orchestrates agentic AI assistants (Claude, Gemini, HuggingFace agents) to propose, validate, and document architecture decisions. A central FlowRunner and governance engines execute flows while agents consume packaged skills and a structured knowledge base (cas-knowledge) of rules, patterns, signals, and decisions. CI/CD workflows trigger agentic builds and synchronise governance state back into agent configuration files.

agents.name: FlowRunner
agents.role: Central orchestrator that executes agentic flows by stepping through a pipeline and mutating shared context.

agents.name: VerifierSubagent
agents.role: Independent validation agent that checks outputs produced by other agents, enforcing correctness.

agents.name: GovernanceActionEngine
agents.role: Executes governed transitions between architecture states using a transition registry, enforcing allowed state changes.

agents.name: ComplianceEngine
agents.role: Evaluates agent proposals against rules and constraints, producing compliance findings and risk assessments.

agents.name: AgenticMerger
agents.role: Merges governance blocks and agent outputs back into the knowledge base and configuration files.

agents.name: SkillAgents
agents.role: Reusable capability packages that provide agents with focused instructions and tool protocols (feature changes, audits, diagram generation, refactors).

orchestration.description: The FlowRunner provides centralised, sequential pipeline execution; GitHub Actions workflows trigger agentic builds and steering syncs; skills act as distributable capability packages that agents can invoke independently. Centralised control is combined with CI/CD-driven async orchestration and skill-based decentralised execution.

tools_and_integrations.purpose: Unified LLM provider abstraction for agent inference and reasoning, enabling provider portability.

tools_and_integrations.name: MockLLMClient
tools_and_integrations.purpose: Deterministic substitute for LiteLLM in tests and evals, ensuring reproducible agent behaviour.

tools_and_integrations.name: GitHub Actions Workflows
tools_and_integrations.purpose: CI/CD triggers for agentic builds, validation, steering sync, and skill evaluations.

tools_and_integrations.name: Skills Packages
tools_and_integrations.purpose: Reusable capability bundles providing instruction sets and tool protocols for specific agent tasks.

tools_and_integrations.name: MkDocs Portal
tools_and_integrations.purpose: Publishes architecture governance documentation as a navigable portal (cas-portal-publish).

tools_and_integrations.name: HuggingFace CLI
tools_and_integrations.purpose: Provider-specific tool integration for HuggingFace-backed agent operations.

state_and_memory.description: cas-knowledge/ holds global rules, patterns, signals, decisions, models, and narratives that act as long-term agent memory.
cas-knowledge/projects/ stores per-project knowledge, separating project-specific context from global governance.
cas-knowledge/runtime/ holds execution profile, rule context, and traces that coordinate current agent executions.
Templates in cas-knowledge/templates/ define the structure of derived outputs (ADRs, patterns, signals) that agents must conform to.
Governance models (GovernanceInventory, GovernanceHealth, GovernanceThroughput) capture the state of governance as traceable metrics.

patterns.name: LLM Provider Abstraction with Mock Fallback

tool_protocols.notes: No evidence of MCP or native tool-calling protocols; LLM interaction is via LiteLLM client abstraction only.

optimisation_targets.notes: Provider abstraction targets cost optimisation by enabling provider swaps without agent code changes.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Abstracting the LLM behind a small client contract limits dependence on vendor-specific features, favouring simple, portable agent execution.

patterns.summary: Agents interact with LLMs exclusively through a thin LiteLLM client abstraction, with a deterministic mock client for testing.
patterns.intent: Decouple agent reasoning from any specific LLM provider so agents can run against different backends (or mocks) without code changes.
patterns.context: Appears in src/cas_runner/llm/ where LiteLLMClient and MockLLMClient implement the same interface, consumed by FlowRunner and governance engines.
patterns.solution: Define a client contract with LiteLLMClient as the production implementation and MockLLMClient as a deterministic substitute. All agent-facing calls go through this interface, allowing swaps and enabling offline evaluations.
implementation_signals: Pair of client classes with identical method signatures (LiteLLMClient/MockLLMClient)
Client chosen through configuration or injection, not hardcoded in agent logic

benefits: Deterministic tests and evals via mock backend
Cost control by selecting cost-optimal providers
costs: Small indirection layer
Provider-specific features not exposed to agents
failure_modes: Mock/client contract drift if interfaces diverge
Provider-specific capabilities required by agent prompts may be unavailable through the abstraction

patterns.reuse_notes: Adopt a minimal LLM client interface with a mock implementation whenever agents need testable, provider-portable reasoning.

patterns.name: Skill-Based Capability Packages

tool_protocols.notes: Skills bundle instructions and tool references; no explicit MCP or native tool-calling protocols observed.

optimisation_targets.notes: Packaging capabilities as skills reduces agent setup overhead and encourages reuse of vetted instructions.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Skills give agents bounded autonomy within well-defined task boundaries, balancing reuse with control.

patterns.summary: Agent capabilities are packaged as self-contained skill directories containing instructions, tool configs, and expected outputs.
patterns.intent: Make agent tasks modular and composable by encapsulating instructions, tool dependencies, and output contracts into reusable skills.
patterns.context: Skills live under .agents/skills/ and .claude/skills/ for feature additions, rule audits, drawio generation, module refactors, and review synchronisation.
forces: Reuse vs. drift between agent platforms
Standardisation vs. flexibility in agent behaviour
patterns.solution: Define a canonical set of skills (cas-add-or-modify-feature, cas-audit-agent-rules, cas-drawio-generator, cas-refactor-knowledge-links, cas-refactor-module, cas-sync-archgov-reviews) that agents can reference. Each skill bundles instructions and expected outputs, enabling agents to execute focused tasks with reduced ambiguity.
implementation_signals: Multiple skill directories under agent config locations ( .agents/skills, .claude/skills)
Skill names follow a consistent 'cas-<task>' naming convention
Skills cross-reference templates and workflows (e.g., cas-sync-archgov-reviews)

evidence.note: Module refactoring skill mirrored for Claude.

benefits: Consistent behaviour across agent platforms when shared via symlinks
costs: Skill maintenance overhead as tasks evolve
Potential duplication across agent config locations
failure_modes: Skill instructions drift from underlying tooling changes
Platform-specific skill variants diverge in behaviour

patterns.reuse_notes: Package any repeated agent task into a structured skill directory with a clear name, scope, and output contract. Verify and maintain skills via eval suites.

patterns.name: Verifier Subagent

tool_protocols.notes: Verification is performed as a dedicated subagent step; no tool-calling protocol observed.

optimisation_targets.notes: The verifier exists to improve output quality and catch errors before governance acceptance.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: A separate verifier narrows agent autonomy by adding an independent validation stage.

patterns.summary: A dedicated verifier subagent independently checks outputs produced by other agents, adding a validation gate before acceptance.
patterns.intent: Introduce an independent check point that catches errors, governance violations, or hallucinated content before results are committed.
patterns.context: Verifier subagent definitions exist for both the .agents (HuggingFace/GoCD) and .claude agent platforms.
forces: Autonomy vs. safety of generated outputs
Cost of double-processing vs. error detection value
patterns.solution: Define a verifier subagent in markdown (verifier.md) that is invoked after other agents produce outputs. The verifier applies governance rules and structural checks, flagging issues for remediation.
implementation_signals: Dedicated verifier.md files in both agent config directories
Verifier referenced in workflow definitions (cas-build-validation.yml)

evidence.note: Verifier subagent definition for Claude platform.
Validation workflow that likely triggers the verifier.

benefits: Reduced risk of unvalidated governance changes
costs: Added latency and cost of a second agent pass
Verifier rules can become outdated
failure_modes: Verifier becomes a rubber-stamp if rules are too permissive
Verifier and producer agents drift apart in understanding

patterns.reuse_notes: Add a verifier subagent whenever agent outputs are committed to shared state and errors would be costly. Keep verifier rules synchronised with governance rules.

patterns.name: Structured Knowledge-Base Memory

tool_protocols.notes: The knowledge base acts as a blackboard that agents read/write; no structured tool protocol is used to query it.

optimisation_targets.notes: Persistent, structured memory reduces hallucination by grounding agent decisions in governance facts.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Structured knowledge constrains agent reasoning to a governed context, limiting autonomy while improving consistency.

patterns.summary: A shared, structured knowledge base (cas-knowledge) acts as long-term agent memory, persisting rules, patterns, signals, decisions, and project context.
patterns.intent: Provide agents with a persistent, queryable source of governance truth to ground decisions and capture learned patterns.
patterns.context: cas-knowledge/ is organised into global/ (rules, patterns, signals, decisions, models, narratives), projects/ (per-project knowledge), and runtime/ (execution context).
patterns.solution: Organise knowledge into global and project scopes with typed buckets (rules, patterns, decisions, signals, models). Agents read from these buckets to constrain actions and write back new learnings (signals, patterns, decisions).
implementation_signals: Typed knowledge directories under cas-knowledge/global/{rules,patterns,signals,decisions,models,narratives}
Template files that define the shape of each knowledge artifact
Runtime rule context (rule-context.json) that agents consult

evidence.note: Runtime rule context consumed by agents.

costs: Knowledge maintenance burden
Querying overhead if context is large
failure_modes: Stale or conflicting rules cause inconsistent agent behaviour
Knowledge sprawl if patterns are not curated

patterns.reuse_notes: Adopt a typed, read/write knowledge base as the blackboard for any multi-project agent system that needs persistent governance memory.

patterns.name: Governance Compliance Engine

tool_protocols.notes: Compliance is checked through a deterministic engine, not a native tool protocol.

optimisation_targets.notes: Enforcing compliance reduces the risk of ungoverned agent behaviour.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Deterministic compliance checks limit agent autonomy by rejecting non-compliant outputs.

patterns.summary: A ComplianceEngine evaluates agent proposals against governance rules, producing findings, metrics, and exception requests.
patterns.intent: Prevent agents from proposing changes that violate established architecture governance by enforcing rules deterministically.
patterns.context: ComplianceEngine sits alongside GovernanceActionEngine and GovernanceActionService in the governance package and produces ComplianceFinding and ComplianceMetrics.
forces: Speed of evaluation vs. depth of review
patterns.solution: Expose a ComplianceEngine that ingests proposed changes, applies rule checks, and emits structured findings (ComplianceFinding) and metrics (ComplianceMetrics). Findings feed into downstream governance actions and exception decisions.
implementation_signals: ComplianceEngine class with explicit rule-check methods
ComplianceFinding and ComplianceMetrics models in governance/models.py
ComplianceEngine referenced by other governance components (ActionService)

benefits: Agents are constrained to compliant actions
costs: Rules must be maintained to stay relevant
Over-strict rules can block legitimate changes
failure_modes: Rules become stale and produce false positives
Compliance overhead reduces agent throughput

patterns.reuse_notes: Implement a deterministic compliance engine wherever agent output has to conform to an evolving rule set; model findings as typed outputs for auditability.

patterns.name: Governance Action Transition Registry

tool_protocols.notes: Transitions are governed by a typed registry, not a dynamic agent protocol.

optimisation_targets.notes: Explicit allowed transitions prevent invalid state changes.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Restricting transitions to registered ones keeps agent state changes predictable.

patterns.summary: A TransitionRegistry enumerates valid governance state transitions, which GovernanceActionEngine executes to keep architecture state changes controlled.
patterns.intent: Encode the set of allowed governance state changes so that agents cannot arbitrarily alter architecture states.
patterns.context: GovernanceActionEngine and TransitionRegistry live in governance/governance_action_engine.py and are backed by GovernanceActionService.
forces: Flexibility of state changes vs. safety
Comprehensiveness of the registry vs. maintenance effort
patterns.solution: Define a TransitionRegistry that lists valid from→to governance state transitions. The GovernanceActionEngine consults this registry before applying any change, rejecting unregistered transitions.
implementation_signals: TransitionRegistry class with explicit transition definitions
GovernanceActionEngine that validates requests against the registry
GovernanceActionService that executes approved actions

evidence.note: Transition registry and engine that enforces allowed state changes.
Service layer for executing governance actions.

benefits: Agents cannot perform arbitrary state changes
costs: Registry must be updated when new transitions are needed
Complex state spaces can make the registry unwieldy
failure_modes: Incomplete registry blocks legitimate actions
Registry and actual governance state drift apart

patterns.reuse_notes: Use an explicit transition registry whenever agents can mutate long-lived governance or architecture state; it provides a guardrail that is easier to audit than ad-hoc validation.

patterns.name: Agentic Governance Merger

tool_protocols.notes: Merging is a deterministic post-processing step, not a tool call.

optimisation_targets.notes: Merge step ensures agent-generated governance content integrates cleanly.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Deterministic merging keeps agent output integration predictable.

patterns.summary: AgenticMerger blends agent-generated governance content back into existing governance files, reconciling new and existing state.
patterns.intent: Integrate agent-produced governance blocks (rules, decisions, patterns) into the persistent governance state without clobbering existing content.
patterns.context: AgenticMerger is used as part of the write-back path when agents propose governance changes, possibly invoked by bootstrap or governance action flows.
forces: Agent output freshness vs. existing governance integrity
Conflicts between agent and human-created content
patterns.solution: AgenticMerger accepts new governance content and merges it into target files, preserving existing content where it does not conflict. This can be reused for config files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) that embed governance blocks.
implementation_signals: AgenticMerger class in governance package
merge functions in bootstrap.py (merge_cas_governance_block, merge_claude_settings) that use similar logic

evidence.note: Similar merge logic used during bootstrapping.

costs: Merge conflicts can still occur with complex edits
Need for merge strategy tuning
failure_modes: Silent loss of agent content due to merge priority
Conflicting blocks merged into inconsistent state

patterns.reuse_notes: Reuse a deterministic merge component whenever agents write back to shared governance or config files; it prevents destructive overwrites.

patterns.name: Runtime Rule Context

tool_protocols.notes: Runtime context is a JSON file that agents and engines read to understand current governance state.

optimisation_targets.notes: Pre-materialised rule context reduces per-call rule loading overhead.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Runtime context constrains agent decisions to current governance facts without hardcoding them.

patterns.summary: A runtime rule-context.json file materialises the current governance rules and expectations for agents to consult during execution.
patterns.intent: Give agents a compact, current snapshot of rules and expectations without requiring them to parse the entire knowledge base.
patterns.context: Stored under cas-knowledge/runtime/ alongside execution-profile.yaml and traces/, the file is updated as governance evolves and read by agents at start of tasks.
forces: Breadth of context vs. prompt/context size limits
Deterministic rule state vs. evolving governance
patterns.solution: Generate and refresh a rule-context.json that summarises the rules agents must heed. Agents load this file at execution start to ground their behaviour, and the file is regenerated after governance changes.
implementation_signals: rule-context.json present in cas-knowledge/runtime/
execution-profile.yaml alongside it to coordinate runtime behaviour
Workflows (cas-managed-steering-sync.yml) that likely update this context

evidence.note: Pre-materialised rule context for agent execution.
Execution profile that likely controls how agents run.

benefits: Reduced prompt length by summarising rules
Clear separation between persistent knowledge and runtime snapshot
costs: Context must be regenerated after rule changes
Stale context can mislead agents
failure_modes: Stale rule-context.json used by agents
Context too large to be useful in prompt

patterns.reuse_notes: Materialise a runtime rule context file whenever agent grounding depends on a large, slowly-changing rule set; regenerate it on rule changes.

patterns.name: Traceable Metric and Trace-Based Observability

tool_protocols.notes: Observability is via traceable metrics and runtime traces, not an agent protocol.

optimisation_targets.notes: Tracing and metrics help detect governance failures and agent misbehaviour.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Traceability constrains agent actions to those that can be recorded and audited.

patterns.summary: Agent and governance actions produce traceable metrics and runtime traces, enabling post-hoc audit of what each agent did and why.
patterns.intent: Capture structured, traceable data around agent actions so governance decisions can be audited and failures diagnosed.
patterns.context: TraceableMetric is defined in governance/models.py, and runtime traces are persisted under cas-knowledge/runtime/traces/. The project also uses opentelemetry for SDK-level tracing.
patterns.solution: Record agent actions and outcomes as TraceableMetrics persisted to runtime traces. Use opentelemetry for SDK-level tracing alongside the domain-specific trace store to give operators a full picture.
implementation_signals: TraceableMetric model in governance/models.py
traces/ directory under cas-knowledge/runtime/
opentelemetry-api and opentelemetry-sdk dependencies in pyproject.toml

costs: Metric collection overhead
Storage and retention of large traces
failure_modes: Incomplete or missing traces for critical actions
Metric definitions drift from actual behaviour

patterns.reuse_notes: Instrument any agentic system with traceable metrics and persisted traces to support governance audit and failure diagnosis; consider opentelemetry for cross-cutting tracing.

patterns.name: Bootstrap Governance Injection

tool_protocols.notes: Governance is injected as static config blocks, not via tool calls.

optimisation_targets.notes: Ensures agents always start with current governance rules, reducing non-compliance.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Bootstrapping constrains agent context with governance, balancing autonomy with guardrails.

patterns.summary: At workspace initialisation, the system injects governance blocks into agent configuration files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md) so every agent starts with current rules.
patterns.intent: Embed governance rules directly into agent bootstrap configuration so agents are grounded in current rules from their first interaction.
patterns.context: bootstrap.py exposes merge_cas_governance_block, merge_claude_settings, and init_workspace, which populate AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and GEMINI.md with governance content.
forces: Governance freshness vs. config file bloat
Uniformity across agent platforms vs. platform-specific config
patterns.solution: On bootstrap, read governance blocks from the knowledge base and merge them into each agent's config file, ensuring the configs are synchronised with current governance. Re-run on governance changes.
implementation_signals: merge_cas_governance_block and merge_claude_settings functions in bootstrap.py
The existence of AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md as generated/merged agent configs
Workflow cas-managed-steering-sync.yml that likely re-runs this sync

evidence.note: Injects governance into agent configuration files.

benefits: Agents always start with current governance
Reduced need for agents to query rule files
costs: Config files can grow large with governance content
Re-sync required on governance changes
failure_modes: Stale config if sync workflow not triggered
Duplicate governance blocks across configs drift apart

patterns.reuse_notes: Inject governance into agent config at bootstrap time if you want agents to be grounded in rules without a live query; pair with a sync workflow.

patterns.name: CI/CD-Driven Agent Pipeline

tool_protocols.notes: Agentic workflows are triggered by CI/CD events; no agent-to-agent tool protocol observed.

optimisation_targets.notes: Automating agentic workflows in CI accelerates governance cycles while enforcing quality gates.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: CI/CD gives agents defined trigger points to run autonomously within a controlled pipeline.

patterns.summary: GitHub Actions workflows (continuous-architecture, build-validation, steering-sync, portal-publish, skill-evals) orchestrate agentic tasks as pipeline steps.
patterns.intent: Trigger agentic governance tasks automatically on repository events, producing validated, publishable results.
patterns.context: Separate workflows handle continuous architecture builds, validation, steering sync, portal publishing, and skill evaluations, all coordinated through GitHub Actions.
patterns.solution: Define dedicated workflows that run agentic skills and governance engines (build, validation, steering sync) and publish results (portal). Each workflow uses composite actions and reusable steps to keep agentic orchestration consistent.
implementation_signals: Multiple cas-*.yml workflows with distinct responsibilities
Shared composite action in .github/actions/setup-cas-env
Validation workflow that checks generated artifacts

evidence.note: Build validation workflow for agentic output.
Syncs steering/governance state back into agent configs.

costs: Workflow maintenance overhead
CI runtime costs for agent tasks
failure_modes: Workflow failures stall governance
Orphaned or overlapping workflows cause duplicate execution

patterns.reuse_notes: Use CI/CD pipelines to drive agentic workflows when tasks are event-triggered and need formal gates (validation, publishing, sync).

patterns.name: Skill Evaluation Suites

tool_protocols.notes: Evals are run through a structured model, not an agent tool protocol.

optimisation_targets.notes: Eval suites ensure skills perform correctly and safely before release.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Skill evals gate skill readiness, limiting unverified autonomy.

patterns.summary: Skills ship with typed evaluation suites (SkillEvalSuite, SkillEvalCase, SkillEvalResult) that validate skill behaviour before use.
patterns.intent: Provide a standard way to measure whether agent skills work as intended, catching regressions early.
patterns.context: Skills are linked to eval suites (SkillEvalSuite with cases and assertions); cas-skill-evals.yml runs these suites in CI.
forces: Skill quality assurance vs. suite authoring effort
patterns.solution: Define SkillEvalCase with SkillAssertions, group into SkillEvalSuite, and run them via the cas-skill-evals workflow to produce SkillEvalReport/SkillEvalResult. Skills are considered ready only when their suites pass.
implementation_signals: models.py defines EvalStatus, SkillAssertions, SkillEvalCase, SkillEvalSuite, SkillEvalResult, SkillEvalReport
cas-skill-evals.yml workflow references skill eval runs
Eval status enum used to gate skill acceptance

costs: Suite authoring overhead
Evals can become stale if skill behaviour changes
failure_modes: Assertions too weak to catch failures
Evaluation suite not run on every skill change

patterns.reuse_notes: Attach typed eval suites to any reusable agent skill and run them in CI to keep skill behaviour trustworthy.

patterns.name: Template-Defined Output Contracts

tool_protocols.notes: Output structure is enforced through markdown templates, not structured schemas.

optimisation_targets.notes: Templates enforce consistent structure, reducing parsing errors and review burden.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Templates constrain agent output format, trading some autonomy for consistency.

patterns.summary: Agents generate artefacts (ADRs, patterns, signals, experiments, learning) conforming to markdown templates that define the expected structure.
patterns.intent: Ensure agent-generated governance artefacts are structured consistently so they can be parsed, reviewed, and reused.
patterns.context: cas-knowledge/templates/ contains architecture_decision_record_template.md, pattern_template.md, signal_template.md, experiment_template.md, learning_template.md, and others.
forces: Flexible agent output vs. structured artefacts
patterns.solution: Maintain a canonical set of artefact templates and require agents to fill them. Templates define sections and expected fields, reducing ambiguity and enabling downstream tooling to consume the artefacts.
implementation_signals: Templates directory with typed markdown files
Skill instructions referencing specific templates (e.g., cas-drawio-generator likely uses diagram_template.md)
Pattern-to-heuristic and promotion templates indicating formal lifecycle

costs: Templates can become stale or overly restrictive
Agents may comply superficially without deep thinking
failure_modes: Agents fill templates incorrectly with hallucinated content
Template sections diverge from actual needs

patterns.reuse_notes: Define artefact templates whenever agents produce documents that are consumed by downstream tools or reviewed by humans; they act as low-friction contracts.

patterns.name: Multi-Provider Agent Configuration Generation

tool_protocols.notes: Each provider gets its own config file (CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, AGENTS.md) that mirrors the same governance.

optimisation_targets.notes: Supporting multiple agents (Claude, Gemini, HuggingFace) improves developer choice and resilience.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Generating per-provider configs standardises governance across autonomous agent platforms.

patterns.summary: The system maintains parallel configuration files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md) that configure different agent platforms with the same governance, synchronised via bootstrap.
patterns.intent: Let the same governance drive agents on multiple AI platforms (Claude, Gemini, HuggingFace) without duplicating governance logic.
patterns.context: Root-level CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, AGENTS.md and corresponding .claude/ and .agents/ directories hold merged governance blocks.
forces: Provider capability differences vs. common contract
patterns.solution: Generate and maintain provider-agnostic governance blocks in each agent's config file (CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, AGENTS.md) via a shared bootstrap process (merge_claude_settings for Claude). Keep all configs in sync when governance changes.
implementation_signals: Multiple root-level agent config files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md)
bootstrap.py has merge_claude_settings and merge_cas_governance_block to inject shared content
Corresponding skill/subagent dirs under .claude/ and .agents/

evidence.note: Claude agent config with governance block.
Gemini agent config with governance block.
Generic agents config with governance block.
Injects shared governance into per-provider configs.

benefits: Governance applied consistently across agent platforms
Developer flexibility in choosing an assistant
costs: Sync/maintenance overhead across configs
Provider-specific features may not surface in shared governance
failure_modes: Configs drift apart if sync not run
Governance blocks become duplicated and inconsistent across files

patterns.reuse_notes: Generate per-provider agent configs from a single governance source if you support multiple AI assistants; automate the sync via bootstrap or CI.

patterns.name: Symlink/Copy Skill Sharing

tool_protocols.notes: Skills are shared between agent directories via symlinks or copies to avoid duplication.

optimisation_targets.notes: Shared skills keep configurations lean and reduce drift between agent platforms.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Centralising skills via sharing reduces the maintenance burden on autonomous agents.

patterns.summary: Skills are shared across agent configuration directories using symlinks or copies (created by _create_symlink_or_copy), preventing duplication and drift.
patterns.intent: Allow agents from different platforms to use the same skill packages without maintaining separate copies.
patterns.context: bootstrap.py's _create_symlink_or_copy is used to place skills under .claude/skills/ and .agents/skills/ from a canonical location.
forces: Single source of truth vs. platform file layout
patterns.solution: At bootstrap time, create symlinks (or copies on platforms where symlinks fail) to share skill directories across agent platform configs, keeping a canonical skill set.
implementation_signals: _create_symlink_or_copy function in bootstrap.py
Duplicate-looking skills dirs under .claude/skills and .agents/skills
Bootstrap called from setup workflow (setup-cas-env)

evidence.note: Creates symlinks or copies to share skills.
Shared skill present in Claude config.
Shared skill present in generic agents config.

costs: Symlinks can break on some platforms
Copies can diverge if not refreshed
failure_modes: Symlink target missing in fresh checkouts
Copy updated in one location but not the other

patterns.reuse_notes: Share skills across agent config directories with symlinks (or copies) to keep a canonical skill set; document the bootstrap step that creates them.

patterns.name: Sequential Flow Runner with Shared Context Propagation

tool_protocols.notes: Orchestration is a direct pipeline of steps; no tool protocol involved.

optimisation_targets.notes: Sequential pipeline with context mutation ensures deterministic step order.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: The runner enforces a fixed step order, trading autonomy for predictability.

patterns.summary: FlowRunner executes a sequential pipeline where a shared context object is passed between steps, each mutating it for the next.
patterns.intent: Provide a deterministic, stepwise execution model for agent flows where each step reads and writes a shared context.
patterns.context: FlowRunner is the central execution entry point in src/cas_runner/runner.py, likely used by CLI and CI workflows to run agent tasks.
forces: Shared context vs. isolation between steps
patterns.solution: Implement FlowRunner so it sequences a defined set of steps, passing a mutable context object from step to step. Steps read required inputs from context and write results back, enabling cumulative state.
implementation_signals: FlowRunner class in runner.py
Expected prepare_inputs contract used by steps
CLI entry point (cli.py#main) invoking the runner

evidence.note: CLI entry point that likely invokes FlowRunner.

costs: Limited adaptive parallelism
Context can grow large across steps
failure_modes: Step failure leaves context in an inconsistent state
Context mutation ordering bugs

patterns.reuse_notes: Use a sequential runner with shared context when agent flows are well-defined and deterministic; it improves debugability but limits dynamic orchestration.

anti_patterns.name: Skill and Config Duplication Across Agent Platforms
symptoms: The same skill (e.g., cas-add-or-modify-feature) appears under both .agents/skills/ and .claude/skills/
Agent config files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md) carry duplicated governance blocks
bootstrap.py needs _create_symlink_or_copy to try to keep copies in sync

where_observed.note: Same skill present in Claude directory.

impact: Doing the same skill in parallel can drift without detection
Governance blocks embedded in multiple configs can diverge, causing inconsistent agent behaviour
Increased maintenance burden for every skill update
suggested_remediation: Use symlinks as the single sharing mechanism instead of copies wherever possible
Centralise skills in a single directory and reference them from agent configs
Add a drift-check CI step that compares governance blocks across config files

anti_patterns.name: Governance Embedded in Human-Facing Agent Config
symptoms: Governance blocks are merged into root files like CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, and GEMINI.md
Bootstrapping is required to re-sync governance after changes
The sync is automated, but failure is silent unless a CI step checks it

where_observed.note: Sync workflow to refresh governance in configs.

impact: Embedded governance becomes stale if sync fails or is bypassed
Humans and agents may read different rule versions if config files drift
Reducing governance to config blocks can hide nuances from agents
suggested_remediation: Keep governance in the knowledge base and reference it, rather than embedding copies
Add a validation step that fails the build if governance blocks in configs are outdated
Provide a single query mechanism for agents to fetch current rules on demand

anti_patterns.name: Stale Pre-Materialised Rule Context
symptoms: A pre-materialised rule-context.json exists but there is no evidence of a hard freshness guarantee
Execution profile and traces are updated separately, so the context can go stale
Agents loading the file may use outdated rules if the sync is missed

where_observed.note: Execution profile that may not be regenerated together with rule context.

impact: Agents make decisions based on outdated governance
Non-compliance is discovered late, at validation time
Debugging becomes harder when context and actual rules differ
suggested_remediation: Regenerate rule-context.json atomically with any governance change
Add a timestamp/version field and validate it at agent startup
Make agents consult the knowledge base for rule changes before acting

anti_patterns.name: CI Workflow Proliferation with Implicit Dependencies
symptoms: Six separate workflows exist (cas-build-steering-projection, cas-build-validation, cas-continuous-architecture, cas-managed-steering-sync, cas-portal-publish, cas-skill-evals)
validate_workflows.py includes checks like check_no_unpinned_installers and check_no_unreachable_dry_run, indicating known CI hygiene issues
Dependencies between workflows are implicit (e.g., steering-sync must run after governance changes)

where_observed.note: Custom validators for CI workflow hardening.

impact: Orchestration of agent pipelines becomes hard to follow
Missed triggers can leave governance in an inconsistent state
Hardcoding and unpinned installers raise security and reproducibility risk
suggested_remediation: Consolidate workflows or make dependencies explicit via a single orchestrator workflow
Adopt composite actions to reduce duplication
Run validate_workflows.py as a mandatory pre-merge check

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Skills use structured instruction packages and templates enforce output shape; agents are grounded via governance blocks and rule context.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Prompt contracts are mostly implicit (markdown templates and skill instructions) rather than typed schemas, which may allow interpretation variability.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: A dedicated verifier subagent plus structured skill eval suites (SkillEvalSuite/SkillEvalCase) and build-validation workflows form layered evaluation.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Evaluation is distributed across subagent verification, skill evals, and CI validation; there is no single central evaluation engine.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Governance is enforced through a compliance engine, transition registry, rule context, and bootstrap-injected governance blocks in agent configs.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Safety is primarily rule-driven and deterministic; human review is supplemented by the verifier, not a formal HITL gate.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: LLM provider abstraction via LiteLLM lets the system select cost-effective providers; mock client reduces eval cost.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: No explicit per-agent cost budgets or throttles were observed; cost management is indirect via provider choice.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Traceable metrics and runtime traces, plus opentelemetry for SDK-level tracing, provide audit and diagnostic data.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Observability is split between domain-specific traces and opentelemetry; no unified dashboard was observed in the source.

open_questions.question: How does FlowRunner handle step failures and context rollback?
open_questions.why_it_matters: A shared mutable context across pipeline steps is only safe if failures are handled deterministically; without rollback, partial state can corrupt downstream steps.
open_questions.evidence_gap: No source file for runner.py internals was available beyond the FlowRunner symbol; no failure-handling evidence could be verified.
open_questions.suggested_next_check: Inspect src/cas_runner/runner.py for exception handling, retry logic, and context reset on failure.

open_questions.question: Are the skills in .agents/skills and .claude/skills actually identical, or do they vary by platform?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The symlink/copy approach only prevents drift if content is truly shared; platform-specific customisations may silently diverge.
open_questions.evidence_gap: Skill file contents were not read; only directory presence was observed.
open_questions.suggested_next_check: Diff the contents of .agents/skills/ and .claude/skills/ to detect divergence; also check if any platform-specific overrides exist.

open_questions.evidence_gap: No explicit approval-required annotation or workflow gate was found in the source symbols.
open_questions.suggested_next_check: Inspect GovernanceActionService and the cas-managed-steering-sync workflow for approval or notification steps.
